title: Raw Sockets
intro: You already await async I/O at work. What you haven't done is see what's underneath it. Eight sessions, and by the last one you're assembling pieces you've already built — not writing an echo server from a blank page.

days.title: A socket is a file descriptor
days.teaser: What socket() actually allocates — and how to go and look at it in /proc.
days.teachBack: Explain what the int from socket() actually is, and what it refers to. Then: a long-running server leaks one fd per connection. Why does it run fine for hours and then fail all at once, and what does it fail with?
days.theoryMarkdown:
### What a socket actually is

The `int` that `socket()` returns is not the socket. It's a **handle** — an index into
your process's file descriptor table, which the kernel uses to find the real thing.

The real thing lives in kernel memory and bundles together:

- the local address and port, once you `bind()`
- the remote address and port, once you `connect()` or `accept()`
- protocol state — for TCP, a whole state machine (`LISTEN`, `SYN_SENT`,
  `ESTABLISHED`, `CLOSE_WAIT`, `TIME_WAIT`, ...) that the kernel drives as packets
  arrive, entirely outside your process and whether or not you ever call `recv()`
- send and receive buffers, which is why the kernel can already be holding bytes for
  you before you ask for them, and why a `recv()` can hand back fewer bytes than were
  sent (Day 5 and Day 6)

So a socket is a live object the kernel maintains for you, and your `int` is a ticket
you hand back every time you want something done with it: `send(fd, ...)`,
`recv(fd, ...)`, `close(fd)`.

That's the same relationship a regular file's fd has to its open-file state. Sockets
were deliberately built to slot into the exact same table as files, pipes and
terminals, so `read`/`write`/`close`/`select` work on all of them almost
interchangeably. That unification is arguably the best design decision in the whole
API — and the reason "everything is a file" is a Unix slogan rather than a technicality.

### Go and look at the table

This is worth thirty seconds, because it turns the paragraph above into something you
have seen rather than something you were told. On Linux, the fd table is exposed as a
directory:

```console
$ ls -l /proc/$$/fd
lrwx------ 1 you you 64 Sep  2 19:04 0 -> /dev/pts/3
lrwx------ 1 you you 64 Sep  2 19:04 1 -> /dev/pts/3
lrwx------ 1 you you 64 Sep  2 19:04 2 -> /dev/pts/3
lrwx------ 1 you you 64 Sep  2 19:04 255 -> /dev/pts/3
```

`$$` is your shell's PID, and there are its three standard fds pointing at a terminal.
Once a process owns a socket, the same listing shows `3 -> socket:[123456]` — that
number in brackets is the kernel object's inode, and it's the actual identity of the
socket. Two processes sharing a socket after `fork()` show the *same* inode under
different fd numbers, which makes the handle-versus-object distinction impossible to
misremember afterwards.

### The call itself

```cpp
int fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
```

Three arguments, three questions:

- **`AF_INET`** — *address family*. What kind of address will this socket use?
  `AF_INET` is IPv4; `AF_INET6` is IPv6; `AF_UNIX` is local-machine-only sockets,
  same syscall, completely different address shape.
- **`SOCK_STREAM`** — *socket type*. What delivery guarantee do you want?
  `SOCK_STREAM` is TCP: reliable, ordered, connection-based byte stream.
  `SOCK_DGRAM` is UDP: fire-and-forget datagrams, no connection.
- **`0`** — *protocol*. Almost always `0`, meaning "the default protocol for that
  family and type", which for `AF_INET` + `SOCK_STREAM` is TCP. You'd set it
  explicitly only in exotic cases, like raw ICMP sockets.

On success you get a small positive int. On failure, `-1`, with `errno` set — the
POSIX pattern of "sentinel return value, look in `errno` for the reason", which is why
`strerror(errno)` will appear in every program in this milestone. `errno` predates
sockets by a decade; it's a 1979-era mechanism that every syscall API since has been
bolted onto.

### A flag most people never learn about

The type argument is not just the type. On Linux you can OR flags into it:

```cpp
int fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM | SOCK_CLOEXEC, 0);
```

`SOCK_CLOEXEC` marks the fd close-on-exec, so it is automatically closed if the process
`exec()`s another program. Without it, every fd you own is inherited by whatever you
launch — so a server that shells out to a helper hands that helper a live copy of its
listening socket. That leaks a resource, and worse, keeps the port occupied by a
process that has no idea it owns it.

You can also set this after the fact with `fcntl(fd, F_SETFD, FD_CLOEXEC)`, and that is
what people did for years. The reason the flag was added directly to `socket()` in 2008
is that the two-call version has a race: between `socket()` returning and `fcntl()`
running, another thread can `fork()` and `exec()`, and the fd escapes anyway. A race
window measured in nanoseconds, closed by moving one bit into the original call.

You don't need it today — this milestone never calls `exec()`. It's here because it's
the kind of detail that separates code that works from code that survives, and because
`accept4()` on Day 4 has the same flag for the same reason.

### Is this still how it works?

Yes, and that's the point of building it by hand. Every mainstream networking stack —
Boost.Asio, Python's `socket`, Node's `net`, Go's `net`, the JVM's NIO — is opening one
of these fds with this syscall at the bottom. Asio's `async_read` ends up calling
`recv()` on an fd it got from `socket()`; what it adds is an event loop so nothing has
to block while waiting. Even Windows agrees: Winsock is a near-clone of this BSD
interface, because by the 1990s everyone had settled on this shape.

What *has* changed in forty years is how you find out a socket is ready without parking
a thread on it: `select()` → `poll()` → `epoll()` → `io_uring` is most of the history of
Linux I/O scalability in one line. But every one of those is about *notification*. None
of them replaced the socket. The fd, and the `socket()`/`bind()`/`connect()` shape, have
been stable since 1983.

### Where the name comes from

"Socket" is a deliberate metaphor from the original Berkeley design (DARPA-funded,
shipped in 4.2BSD in 1983): an endpoint you plug a connection into, like a wall socket
or a phone jack. The API predates HTTP by about eight years, and predates the web as a
concept entirely. TCP/IP on Unix needed a programming interface long before there was a
browser to point at it.

quiz.prompt: What does it mean if socket() returns -1 versus returning 3?

options.text: -1 specifically means the kernel is out of memory
options.why: -1 is generic on purpose. Collapsing every failure into one return value is exactly why errno exists as a second channel: one bit of "it broke", plus a separate "here's which way".

options.text: -1 is failure and errno says why; 3 is a valid fd — the lowest free slot in the table
options.why: Both halves matter. -1 is a sentinel meaning "look at errno" — the specific reason (EMFILE, ENFILE, EACCES, EAFNOSUPPORT) lives there, not in the return value. And 3 isn't arbitrary: POSIX guarantees the lowest available fd, and 0/1/2 are already stdin/stdout/stderr, so a first socket in a normal process is almost always 3. If you ever see 0 come back from socket(), someone closed stdin — which is a real and confusing class of bug.

options.text: -1 is success and 3 is an error code, like functions that return 0 on success
options.why: Inverted, and it's a real confusion because POSIX genuinely has both conventions. Calls that *return a resource* (socket, open, accept) return the resource and use -1 for failure. Calls that only report status (pthread_create and most of the pthreads API) return 0 on success and the error number directly, leaving errno untouched.

options.text: -1 means no client has connected yet; 3 means one has
options.why: socket() hasn't touched the network at all — no address, no port, no packet. It cannot know anything about clients. That's accept()'s job, three days from now.

quiz.prompt: Why is the fd from socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0) not yet listening or connected to anything — what's missing?

options.text: It has no address. socket() allocates the object; bind()/connect() give it a role
options.why: Allocate, then configure, then use — the three-step shape that repeats all over this API. Right now the kernel holds a TCP socket in state CLOSED with no local address, no remote address, and nothing in its buffers.

options.text: The protocol argument is 0, which leaves it unusable until you pass IPPROTO_TCP
options.why: 0 means "the default protocol for this family and type" — which for AF_INET + SOCK_STREAM is exactly IPPROTO_TCP. Passing it explicitly changes nothing at all. You'd only set it for exotic cases like raw ICMP sockets.

options.text: It isn't backed by a file yet, and every fd ultimately refers to a file on disk
options.why: An fd is a handle to any kernel object implementing the file interface — sockets, pipes, terminals, epoll instances, timers, even eventfd. No disk is involved. That unification is the best design decision in the whole API: read/write/close work on all of them.

options.text: Nothing's missing — the kernel already picked an ephemeral port for it
options.why: No port is reserved until bind(), or until connect() does an implicit bind on your behalf. Until then the socket owns no part of the port space, which is why a thousand processes can all call socket() and none of them collide.

quiz.prompt: A program calls socket() ten thousand times in a loop and never calls close(). What actually runs out, and how does it show up?

options.text: Nothing — a socket with no address bound holds no resources until you bind() it
options.why: The kernel allocated a real structure the moment socket() returned: buffers, protocol state, a table slot. "Unbound" only means the address fields are empty. This is the fd leak in a nutshell — it looks free because nothing visible happened.

options.text: Nothing — the kernel reclaims sockets that have no address once memory gets tight
options.why: There's no garbage collector here. The fd is a reference the kernel assumes you still want; it's released when you close it or when the process exits. Process exit is the only free cleanup you get, which is exactly why a long-lived server leaking fds is so much worse than a short script doing it.

options.text: The fd table — you hit RLIMIT_NOFILE and socket() starts returning -1 with errno EMFILE
options.why: Every fd is a slot in a per-process table with a hard ceiling (`ulimit -n`, often 1024 or 8192). The failure is quiet and late: nine thousand calls succeed, then everything fails at once — which is why "check the return value of every syscall" stops sounding paranoid. EMFILE is per-process; ENFILE is the system-wide table, and seeing that one means you've taken the whole machine down, not just yourself.

options.text: The ephemeral port range — 65535 ports means you run out of ports long before fds
options.why: Plausible arithmetic, wrong stage. No port is reserved until bind() or connect(); these sockets never touched the port space. Port exhaustion is real, but it's something you hit by opening lots of *connections* — and it's why TIME_WAIT eventually shows up in your life.

quiz.prompt: SOCK_CLOEXEC exists because doing the same job with a later fcntl() call has a race. What is the race, and what escapes through it?

options.text: Another thread can fork+exec between socket() and fcntl(), and the child inherits the fd
options.why: The window is tiny — two instructions — but a busy multi-threaded server does this constantly, and the consequence is durable: the child holds a live copy of the socket, keeps the port occupied after the parent dies, and has no idea it owns it. That's why the flag was moved into the creating call itself in Linux 2.6.27. accept4(), pipe2(), dup3() and open()'s O_CLOEXEC all exist for exactly this reason.

options.text: fcntl() can fail, and code that ignores its return value leaves the flag unset
options.why: True and worth checking, but that's an unchecked-error bug, not a race — it behaves identically every time you run it. A race needs a second thread of execution whose timing changes the outcome.

options.text: Signals can interrupt fcntl() and leave the descriptor in a half-configured state
options.why: fcntl(F_SETFD) doesn't block, so there's nothing for a signal to interrupt, and descriptor flags aren't partially applied. EINTR is a real and irritating part of this API, but it belongs to blocking calls like recv() and accept().

options.text: The kernel may reuse the fd number in another thread before fcntl() runs
options.why: It can't. The fd is allocated to your process the moment socket() returns; nothing else gets that number until it's closed. Allocation is atomic — that part was never the problem.

quiz.prompt: When Asio hands you `co_await socket.async_read_some(...)`, what has replaced the raw recv() call underneath?

options.text: Asio uses a userspace TCP stack to skip the syscall, which is where the speedup comes from
options.why: Kernel-bypass stacks exist (DPDK, and the reason people say "userspace TCP"), but they're a specialist tool for line-rate packet processing and Asio isn't one. Ordinary Asio is a thin, portable wrapper over the kernel's sockets.

options.text: io_uring replaced the socket API — modern async I/O submits operations directly, with no fd
options.why: io_uring changed how you *submit and complete* work, not what you operate on: its ops take the same fd from the same socket() call. Forty years in, the notification mechanism has been rewritten four times and the socket abstraction hasn't moved.

options.text: It's the same recv(), but Asio runs it on a worker thread so the blocking wait is off your coroutine
options.why: That's the thread-pool model — real, and what some libraries genuinely do, but it's the design Asio exists to avoid. A thread parked in a blocking recv() costs a stack and a context switch per connection; readiness notification costs one epoll entry. That difference is precisely why C10k was a named problem.

options.text: Nothing — it's still recv() on an fd from socket(); what Asio adds is knowing when to call it
options.why: This is the whole point of Day 1. Asio owns an event loop (epoll on Linux, kqueue on BSD, IOCP on Windows) that watches the fd and resumes your coroutine once the kernel says data has arrived — then does the ordinary recv(). The abstraction you already use at work is a scheduler bolted onto the exact calls in this milestone.

task.markdown:
Write a program that:

1. Calls `socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0)`
2. Checks the return value — on failure, print `strerror(errno)` and exit non-zero
3. On success, prints the fd
4. Calls `close(fd)` before exiting

That's the whole program. No address, no `bind()`, no network activity yet.

Then, before you close it, find your socket in the fd table. Add a
`std::getchar();` right before the `close()` so the process waits, run it, and in
another terminal:

```console
$ ls -l /proc/$(pgrep -n day1)/fd
```

You should see your fd pointing at `socket:[...]`. Predict the fd number before you
look. Then take the `getchar()` back out.

- You'll need `<unistd.h>` for `close()`, `<cstring>` for `strerror`, and
  `<cerrno>` for `errno`, alongside `<sys/socket.h>`
checklist: `socket()` return value checked before use
`strerror(errno)` printed on failure
non-zero exit status on failure
`close(fd)` called on success
found the fd in `/proc/<pid>/fd`, and predicted its number correctly
zero warnings under `-Wall -Wextra`

days.title: Addresses and byte order
days.teaser: Why sockaddr_in carries eight bytes of deliberate padding, and why htons() compiles to nothing on half the machines ever built.
days.teachBack: Explain why network byte order exists at all — what would break if every machine just sent its integers however it stores them. Then: which fields of sockaddr_in need htons/htonl and which don't, and how would you know without looking it up?
days.theoryMarkdown:
### `sockaddr_in`: the address socket() was missing

Day 1 left the fd with no address — the kernel had a TCP socket in state `CLOSED`,
allocated but unconfigured. `bind()`, three days from now, needs an address to give it,
and that address is a struct:

```cpp
struct sockaddr_in {
    sa_family_t    sin_family;   // AF_INET
    in_port_t      sin_port;     // port, in network byte order
    struct in_addr sin_addr;     // IPv4 address, in network byte order
    unsigned char  sin_zero[8];  // padding — see below
};
```

Four fields, and every one of them is trying to solve a different problem.

### `struct sockaddr`: the shape everything gets cast to

`bind()`, `connect()`, and `accept()` don't take a `sockaddr_in *`. They take a
`sockaddr *` — a *generic* address struct that's supposed to work for `AF_INET`,
`AF_INET6`, `AF_UNIX`, and anything else anyone invents later:

```cpp
struct sockaddr {
    sa_family_t sa_family;    // address family — AF_INET, AF_INET6, AF_UNIX, ...
    char        sa_data[14];  // protocol-specific address — opaque at this type
};
```

You never construct one of these directly. It exists purely as the type these calls are
declared to take, so that one function signature can accept any address family without
C needing a concept of inheritance. `sa_data` is 14 bytes of "whatever the real struct
needs there" — from `sockaddr`'s own point of view, meaningless bytes.

### Why `sin_zero` is there at all

C has no inheritance, so in 1983 the answer was: make every address-family-specific
struct exactly the same *size* as the generic one, and let callers cast between the
pointer types. `sin_zero` is filler that exists purely to pad `sockaddr_in` out to
match `sizeof(struct sockaddr)` — it carries no data and you never read it. It's the
C-shaped version of a base class, four decades before anyone would call it that.

The arithmetic is exact, and worth doing once by hand. `sockaddr` is 2 bytes of family
plus 14 bytes of data — 16 bytes total. `sockaddr_in`'s real fields are 2 bytes of
family, 2 of port, 4 of address — 8 bytes, less than half of what `sockaddr` promises
callers they can rely on being there. `sin_zero`'s 8 bytes exist to make up the
difference: `8 + 8 = 16`, matching `sockaddr` exactly. On this machine:

```cpp
sizeof(struct sockaddr)    // 16
sizeof(struct sockaddr_in) // 16 — matches, which is the whole point
```

(`sockaddr_in6`, for IPv6, is a different size again — which is exactly why every one
of these calls also takes an explicit length parameter alongside the pointer. The
struct can't tell you its own size once it's been cast to the generic type.)

Since `sin_zero` carries no data and you never touch it by name, the idiom everywhere is
to zero the whole struct up front rather than set every field yourself:

```cpp
void *memset(void *s, int c, size_t n);
```

```cpp
sockaddr_in addr;
std::memset(&addr, 0, sizeof(addr));   // sin_zero handled; every other field about to be overwritten anyway
addr.sin_family = AF_INET;
```

One call, `sin_zero` is correctly zero, and you never have to think about the padding
field by name again.

### Byte order: the actual problem being solved

`sin_port` and `sin_addr` are multi-byte integers, and a multi-byte integer has no
single obvious way to sit in memory. Take the port `9000`, decimal — in hex that's
`0x2328`. A CPU has to decide which byte goes at the lower address: the `0x23` or the
`0x28`. Intel chips (and ARM, in its usual mode) put the *least* significant byte
first — **little-endian**. Older Motorola and SPARC chips did the opposite —
**big-endian**. Neither is "correct"; they're just two equally valid conventions that
different hardware vendors picked independently.

That's fine as long as a number never leaves the machine that produced it. The moment
two different computers need to agree on what bytes on the wire *mean*, they need to
agree on an order — otherwise a little-endian machine sends `9000` and a big-endian
machine reads it back as `9217`. The internet's answer, baked into TCP/IP from the
start, is: **network byte order is always big-endian**, full stop, regardless of what
either endpoint's CPU prefers internally. Four functions convert between the two, and
they only ever differ in direction and width:

```cpp
uint16_t htons(uint16_t hostshort);  // host  -> network, 16-bit (ports)
uint32_t htonl(uint32_t hostlong);   // host  -> network, 32-bit (addresses)
uint16_t ntohs(uint16_t netshort);   // network -> host, 16-bit
uint32_t ntohl(uint32_t netlong);    // network -> host, 32-bit
```

`h`/`n` is which side you're converting *from*; `s`/`l` is *short* (16-bit) or *long*
(32-bit). Read the name and you already know the signature. In use, filling in the two
multi-byte fields of yesterday's struct:

```cpp
sockaddr_in addr{};
addr.sin_family = AF_INET;
addr.sin_port = htons(9000);              // host uint16_t -> network order
addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(INADDR_ANY); // host uint32_t -> network order
```

and undoing it on the way back, once you have a peer's address to print (Day 4):

```cpp
uint16_t port = ntohs(peer.sin_port);     // network order -> host uint16_t, e.g. 9000
```

Here's the detail that trips people up the first time: on a big-endian machine,
`htons()` has nothing to do — the native order and the network order are already the
same — so it's typically defined to literally return its argument unchanged. It still
compiles, still runs, still "works" if you forget to call it on a little-endian box
and test only on a big-endian one. That asymmetry is exactly how byte-order bugs used
to hide from a whole team for months: it worked on one architecture and silently
corrupted data on another.

### `INADDR_ANY` vs. a literal address

`sin_addr` needs a value too. `INADDR_ANY` (numerically `0.0.0.0`) doesn't mean "no
address" — it tells the kernel *"accept connections arriving on any of this machine's
network interfaces,"* which matters the moment a box has more than one (a LAN
interface and a Wi-Fi interface, say, or a container's internal bridge alongside its
host-facing one). Binding to a literal IP instead restricts you to traffic that
arrived on that one specific interface. A server binds `INADDR_ANY` almost always; a
literal address shows up when a machine deliberately wants to be reachable on only one
of its networks.

### A sharp edge in the API you're about to use

```cpp
char *inet_ntoa(struct in_addr in);
```

`inet_ntoa()` turns a `struct in_addr` back into a printable string, and its return
type is the trap: a `char *` into a **static buffer owned by the library** — not
memory you allocated, and not memory that's yours alone.

```cpp
printf("%s\n", inet_ntoa(a));                    // fine on its own
printf("%s %s\n", inet_ntoa(a), inet_ntoa(b));   // prints the SAME text twice — whichever
                                                  // call the compiler happened to run last
```

Call it twice before using the first result and you get the same pointer back both
times, holding whichever address was converted most recently — C++ doesn't even
guarantee which of the two `inet_ntoa()` calls in that second line runs first, so you
can't reliably predict *which* address wins, only that both printed values will match.
This is a very old API
(pre-thread-safety as a design concern at all), which is exactly why its replacement
takes a caller-supplied buffer instead:

```cpp
const char *inet_ntop(int af, const void *restrict src,
                       char *restrict dst, socklen_t size);
```

```cpp
char text[INET_ADDRSTRLEN];               // 16 bytes — big enough for any IPv4 text form
inet_ntop(AF_INET, &addr.sin_addr, text, sizeof(text));
printf("%s\n", text);                     // yours; a second call elsewhere can't touch it
```

You'll likely still run into `inet_ntoa()` in code older than you are; know what it's
actually handing back before you trust it. `inet_ntop()`'s counterpart going the other
direction, `inet_pton()` (text to binary), is Day 7's tool once you're building
addresses to `connect()` to rather than just printing ones you received.

### Is any of this still how it's done?

The byte-order rule, yes, completely — every IP packet, every TCP header, every DNS
message on the internet today is big-endian on the wire, unchanged since the 1970s
ARPANET days, regardless of what's inside your phone or your laptop. What's changed is
how much of this you touch by hand: `getaddrinfo()` (a level up from what you're doing
this week, and a fair bit more machinery than one function signature is worth showing
here) hides most manual byte-order juggling behind name resolution, doing both DNS
lookup and struct-filling in one call. You're doing it by hand this week for the same
reason as Day 1 — so the abstraction is a convenience later, not a black box.

### The Great Endian War

The terms "big-endian" and "little-endian" aren't engineering jargon invented for this
— they're a deliberate joke. In 1980, Danny Cohen wrote an internet-famous paper called
*"On Holy Wars and a Plea for Peace,"* borrowing the words straight from *Gulliver's
Travels*, where the empires of Lilliput and Blefuscu go to actual war over which end
of a soft-boiled egg you're supposed to crack. His point was that the byte-order
argument between hardware vendors was exactly that pointless — two functionally
equivalent conventions, fought over as if one were obviously correct. The joke stuck so
well that it's now the only name anyone uses, in every networking textbook and every
RFC that has to specify it.

quiz.prompt: What problem does network byte order actually solve — what goes wrong without it?

options.text: It stops a malicious host from spoofing another machine's IP address
options.why: That's a routing and authentication problem, solved (imperfectly) by things entirely outside this struct — ingress filtering, TLS, etc. Byte order just makes sure a correctly-sent number is read correctly; it has no opinion on whether the sender is who it claims to be.

options.text: Different CPUs store multi-byte integers in different orders; without an agreed wire order, two machines misread each other's numbers
options.why: Little-endian and big-endian are both legitimate, and neither machine is "wrong" internally. The problem only exists at the boundary: if a little-endian sender puts its native byte order straight on the wire, a big-endian receiver reads the same bytes back as a different number. Network byte order is just an agreed convention (big-endian) that both sides convert to and from, so the bytes on the wire mean the same thing regardless of either machine's internals.

options.text: It lets the same sockaddr_in struct work for both IPv4 and IPv6 connections
options.why: That's a different problem, solved a different way — sockaddr_in6 is a separate, larger struct, and the generic sockaddr cast (with sin_zero padding it to match) is what lets one pointer type stand in for either. Byte order doesn't touch which address family a struct represents.

options.text: It compresses multi-byte values so addresses and ports take fewer bytes on the wire
options.why: Byte order and size are unrelated. A 16-bit port is 2 bytes in host order and 2 bytes in network order — htons() rearranges which byte goes where, it doesn't drop or pack anything.

quiz.prompt: sin_zero is 8 bytes of padding in sockaddr_in. What is it padding *to*, and why does that matter for a function like bind()?

options.text: It pads sockaddr_in to the same size as the generic sockaddr struct, which is the type bind() actually takes
options.why: C has no inheritance, so 1983's answer to "one function, many address types" was to make every family-specific struct the same size as the generic one and cast pointers between them. bind()/connect()/accept() all take a `sockaddr *`; sin_zero is what makes that cast harmless for sockaddr_in specifically. It carries no data — you never read it, only zero it.

options.text: It's memory the kernel reads as behavior flags, so leaving it nonzero can silently change how bind() behaves
options.why: The kernel doesn't read sin_zero as flags for AF_INET at all — it's ignored content, not a hidden control channel. You zero it as a hygiene habit (uninitialized stack memory is not something to hand the kernel), not because leaving garbage in it changes behavior.

options.text: It pads the struct to a multiple of 8 bytes so the CPU can access it with aligned loads
options.why: A plausible-sounding reason, since padding often is about alignment — but not this padding. sin_zero's size was chosen to match sockaddr's size, not any CPU alignment boundary; the struct isn't defined in terms of a target architecture's word size at all.

options.text: It reserves space for IPv6 fields so old code keeps working when a socket upgrades to IPv6
options.why: sockaddr_in never becomes an IPv6 address — sockaddr_in6 is a wholly separate struct with its own (larger) size, used with AF_INET6. Nothing about sin_zero anticipates or enables that; there's no upgrade path through it.

quiz.prompt: On a big-endian machine, what does htons() actually do to its argument, and why is that a dangerous thing to build a testing habit around?

options.text: It still swaps the bytes, just using the opposite swap direction from a little-endian machine
options.why: There's nothing to swap: if host order and network order are already the same sequence of bytes, a "swap" would introduce a difference where none is needed. htons() is defined to be a no-op precisely when the two orders agree.

options.text: It converts the integer to a floating-point representation so it survives cross-platform math
options.why: Byte order and numeric representation (integer vs. float) are unrelated concerns. htons() only ever rearranges the bytes of the integer you gave it — it never changes what type of value it is.

options.text: It's undefined behavior on big-endian machines, since the macro assumes a little-endian host
options.why: htons() is portable and well-defined on every architecture — that's the entire point of using it instead of hand-rolling a byte swap. It behaves correctly (as a no-op) on big-endian and correctly (as a real swap) on little-endian; nothing about calling it is ever undefined.

options.text: It returns the value unchanged, because native order already equals network order — so forgetting to call it can look correct on that one architecture
options.why: htons() only has work to do when host order differs from network order. On a big-endian box those already match, so a build that skips the conversion entirely can still produce byte-for-byte correct output there — and then corrupt every port and address the moment the same code runs on a little-endian machine. Testing on one architecture doesn't prove the conversion is actually happening.

quiz.prompt: What does binding to INADDR_ANY actually mean, in terms of what the kernel does differently versus binding to one specific literal address?

options.text: INADDR_ANY delays choosing an address until the first connection arrives, then binds to whichever interface it came in on
options.why: bind() takes effect immediately when you call it — there's no deferred binding. INADDR_ANY isn't "decide later," it's "don't filter by local address at all," and the socket is fully bound (to the port, on every interface) before any connection exists.

options.text: INADDR_ANY makes the socket accept both UDP and TCP traffic on the same port
options.why: The socket's type (SOCK_STREAM vs. SOCK_DGRAM) was fixed back at socket() and has nothing to do with which address you bind. INADDR_ANY only affects which interfaces' traffic the kernel delivers to this socket, not what protocol it speaks.

options.text: INADDR_ANY reserves the port on every machine on the local network, not just this one
options.why: Port numbers are a per-machine namespace; there's no mechanism by which binding a socket on one host reserves anything on another. INADDR_ANY only widens which of *this* machine's interfaces the socket listens on.

options.text: The kernel accepts connections arriving on any of the machine's network interfaces, instead of only the one owning a specific address
options.why: A machine with a LAN interface and a Wi-Fi interface — or a container's internal bridge alongside its host-facing one — has more than one local address. INADDR_ANY tells the kernel not to filter by which interface traffic arrived on; a literal address restricts the socket to whichever interface actually owns that address.

quiz.prompt: inet_ntoa() returns a char*. What are you not allowed to assume about that pointer, and what breaks if you call it twice before using the first result?

options.text: It's heap-allocated per call, and you must free() it yourself or you leak memory
options.why: The opposite problem would be safer than the real one. You don't own this pointer and must never free() it — it's static storage inside the library, reused forever, not something malloc'd on your behalf.

options.text: It returns a fresh buffer on every call, which makes it fully safe to use from multiple threads at once
options.why: Backwards — the shared static buffer is exactly why inet_ntoa() is not thread-safe. Two threads calling it concurrently can each see a mix of the other's address text, which is precisely the class of bug inet_ntop() was introduced to eliminate.

options.text: It points into a static buffer owned by the library; a second call overwrites it, so both calls end up pointing at the same (second) text
options.why: This is an old, pre-thread-safety-as-a-design-concern API. The buffer is shared and reused on every call, not allocated per-call. `printf("%s %s", inet_ntoa(a), inet_ntoa(b))` is a classic trap — by the time printf reads the first %s, both pointers refer to the same buffer holding b's text, so it prints b twice. inet_ntop(), which writes into a buffer you supply, exists specifically to fix this.

options.text: The string is only valid until the socket that produced the address is closed
options.why: The pointer's validity has nothing to do with any socket's lifetime — it's tied entirely to the next call to inet_ntoa() from anywhere in the process, which overwrites the same static buffer regardless of what sockets are open or closed.

days.title: bind() and listen()
days.teaser: Break your own port on purpose, then find the option that fixes it — and the one letter that turns it into kernel load balancing.
days.teachBack: The backlog you pass to listen() is a queue of what, exactly — and who puts things in it? Then explain why the port was still busy after you killed the server, and what SO_REUSEADDR is actually overriding.
days.theoryMarkdown:
### Two calls, two completely different jobs

Day 1 gave you a socket with no address. Day 2 built the address. Today they meet, and
then a second call turns the result into something that can receive connections.

```cpp
bind(fd, reinterpret_cast<sockaddr *>(&addr), sizeof(addr));
listen(fd, 128);
```

`bind()` is the claim: *this socket owns port 9000 on these interfaces.* From the moment
it returns, no other socket can hold that same (address, port) pair — the kernel keeps a
table of bound endpoints, and yours is now in it. That's the whole job. A bound socket
still can't accept anything.

`listen()` is the state change. It takes the socket from "has an address" to
`LISTEN` — the TCP state machine from Day 1 finally starts running. The kernel begins
answering SYN packets on that port on your behalf, completing handshakes *without your
process being involved at all*, and stacking the finished connections somewhere for you
to collect later.

That "somewhere" is the interesting part.

### The backlog is a queue of finished handshakes

The second argument to `listen()` is the backlog, and almost everyone's first guess
about what it queues is wrong. It is not a queue of bytes, and it is not a limit on how
many clients you can serve. It's the depth of the queue of **connections the kernel has
already completed the three-way handshake for, which your code has not yet called
`accept()` on.**

Read that again, because it has a consequence people find genuinely surprising: a client
can `connect()` successfully, send data, and get an acknowledgement, all while your
server is busy elsewhere and has never heard of it. The handshake is the kernel's
business, not yours. `accept()` doesn't create the connection — it hands you one the
kernel finished earlier.

So the backlog is a shock absorber. If ten clients connect during the second your
process spends serving someone else, they sit in that queue and get accepted as soon as
you come back around. If the queue is full when an eleventh arrives, the kernel's
behaviour depends on configuration, but the usual outcome on Linux is that it drops the
SYN, and the client's TCP stack retries a moment later — so the client sees a slow
connect rather than a refused one.

Linux actually keeps two queues here: a SYN queue for handshakes *in progress* and an
accept queue for handshakes that are *done*. The backlog argument sizes the second one.
(The split exists partly because of SYN flood attacks — a trivially cheap DoS where an
attacker sends handshake openings and never completes them, filling a single combined
queue with garbage. SYN cookies, which let the kernel forget about half-open connections
entirely and reconstruct them from the client's reply, were invented in 1996 for exactly
this.)

### Your backlog number is a suggestion

Pass `listen(fd, 4096)` and you will very likely not get 4096. Linux silently clamps the
value to `net.core.somaxconn`, and it does not tell you:

```console
$ cat /proc/sys/net/core/somaxconn
4096
```

That default was `128` for most of Linux's history and only changed to `4096` in kernel
5.4 (2019) — which means a decade of servers all over the internet were quietly running
with a backlog two orders of magnitude smaller than the number in their source code.
Nothing warns you. The call succeeds either way.

### Reproducing "Address already in use" on purpose

This is the classic restart failure, and the usual folklore version of it —
*"start the server, kill it, start it again, and bind fails"* — is **wrong**. Try it
with a server that has only ever listened, and the restart works fine. A listening
socket with no connections through it releases its port the moment the process dies.

What actually holds the port is a *connection*, not a listener. When a TCP connection
closes, the endpoint that closed **first** parks in `TIME_WAIT` for a couple of minutes,
holding its (address, port) pair so that stray packets from the dead connection can't be
delivered into a fresh one that happens to reuse the same numbers. If your server closed
a client's connection before it died, the server's own port is what's sitting in
`TIME_WAIT`, and the restart fails:

```
bind FAILED: Address already in use
```

So to reproduce it deliberately you need three things, in order: a client that connects,
a server that closes that connection, and only then a restart.

### SO_REUSEADDR, and the part nobody mentions

The fix is a socket option, set **before** `bind()` — it changes what `bind()` is
allowed to do, so setting it afterwards accomplishes nothing:

```cpp
int yes = 1;
setsockopt(fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, &yes, sizeof(yes));
```

Now the part that will otherwise waste an hour of your evening. On Linux, **both** the
lingering `TIME_WAIT` socket and the new one have to carry `SO_REUSEADDR` for the bind
to be allowed. The connection your server accepted inherits its options from the
listening socket it came from — so the flag on the `TIME_WAIT` socket is whatever the
*previous run* of your server had set.

The consequence is genuinely confusing the first time: you hit `EADDRINUSE`, you add
`SO_REUSEADDR`, you rebuild, you restart — and it fails again, because the socket
holding the port was created by the old binary that didn't set it. Run it once more and
it works, and will keep working forever after. Verified, on this exact question:

| Previous run set `SO_REUSEADDR`? | Restart *with* `SO_REUSEADDR` |
| --- | --- |
| no | `EADDRINUSE` — still refused |
| yes | binds immediately |

There's one more case where the option can't save you at all. If the *client* never
closed its end, the connection isn't in `TIME_WAIT` — it's in `FIN_WAIT2`, which is a
live connection still waiting on the other side's FIN, not a lingering corpse.
`SO_REUSEADDR` only forgives `TIME_WAIT`. A half-closed connection holds the port until
the client goes away or `tcp_fin_timeout` (60 seconds, by default) expires.

### The one letter that changes everything

`SO_REUSEADDR` has a near-twin: **`SO_REUSEPORT`**, added in Linux 3.9 (2013), and it
does something completely different despite the almost identical name. It lets *multiple
separate sockets — in multiple separate processes —* bind the exact same port
simultaneously, and has the kernel load-balance incoming connections across them by
hashing each connection's four-tuple.

That is a genuinely big deal. It's how you scale an accept loop across CPU cores without
a single thread doing all the accepting and handing work off: run N identical processes,
each with its own listening socket on port 80, and the kernel distributes the
connections. NGINX, HAProxy and Envoy all have a flag for it. It also enables
zero-downtime restarts — the new process binds the same port before the old one exits,
so no connection is ever refused in the gap.

You don't need it for this milestone. You should know it's one letter away from the
option you *are* using.

### Go and look at the listening socket

Once `listen()` has run, the socket is visible from outside your process:

```console
$ ss -ltn
State    Recv-Q   Send-Q   Local Address:Port   Peer Address:Port
LISTEN   0        128            0.0.0.0:9000        0.0.0.0:*
```

`ss` is the modern replacement for `netstat` (same information, reads
`/proc/net/tcp` far more efficiently). `-l` is listening sockets, `-t` is TCP, `-n`
skips DNS resolution so you see numbers instead of hostnames.

On a `LISTEN` row those two queue columns are repurposed and worth knowing: **`Recv-Q`
is the number of connections currently sitting in the accept queue waiting for you**,
and **`Send-Q` is the backlog you actually got** — the clamped value, not the number you
passed. That's how you check what `somaxconn` did to your argument without guessing.

`0.0.0.0` in the local address is `INADDR_ANY` from Day 2, printed back at you.

quiz.prompt: The backlog argument to listen() is the depth of a queue. A queue of what, exactly — and who puts things in it?

options.text: Half-finished handshakes — clients that sent a SYN but haven't completed the exchange
options.why: Very close, and Linux does keep exactly that queue — but it's the *other* one. The SYN queue holds handshakes in progress; the accept queue holds finished ones, and the backlog argument sizes the accept queue. The split exists partly so SYN floods can't crowd out completed connections.

options.text: Bytes that have arrived on established connections but haven't been read yet
options.why: That's the socket receive buffer, and it's per-connection — each accepted socket has its own. The backlog is counted in whole connections, not bytes, and it belongs to the listening socket rather than to any one client.

options.text: The maximum number of clients the server can have connected at one time
options.why: A common misreading, and it would make listen(fd, 5) a five-client server. Once you accept() a connection it leaves the queue entirely, so the backlog limits how many can be *waiting to be accepted* at once, not how many you can serve. Concurrent connection count is bounded by your fd limit, not this.

options.text: Connections the kernel has already completed the handshake for, which you haven't accept()ed yet — the kernel fills it, not your code
options.why: This is the fact that reorders how you think about accept(). The kernel answers SYNs and completes three-way handshakes on your behalf, with your process asleep or busy elsewhere, and stacks the finished connections in this queue. accept() doesn't create a connection; it hands you one the kernel finished earlier. Which is why a client can connect() successfully and even send data to a server that has never heard of it.

quiz.prompt: You call listen(fd, 4096) and it returns 0. Why might your actual backlog be far smaller than 4096, and how would you find out what you really got?

options.text: listen() rounds the backlog down to the nearest power of two
options.why: No rounding rule like that exists — and 4096 is already a power of two, so it wouldn't explain a smaller effective value anyway. The limit is an administrator-set ceiling, not an arithmetic adjustment.

options.text: It isn't smaller — a successful listen() means you got exactly the backlog you asked for
options.why: This is the assumption the clamping punishes. A zero return means the call was accepted, not that the argument was honoured; the kernel silently takes min(backlog, somaxconn) and reports success regardless.

options.text: The backlog shrinks as connections are accepted, and only refills when the server goes idle
options.why: The backlog is a fixed ceiling on queue depth, not a consumable budget. Accepting a connection frees a slot immediately; nothing has to go idle for the queue to accept new arrivals.

options.text: Linux silently clamps it to net.core.somaxconn; ss -ltn shows the effective value in Send-Q on the LISTEN row
options.why: The call succeeds either way and never warns you, which is what makes this bite. somaxconn defaulted to 128 for most of Linux's history and only became 4096 in kernel 5.4 (2019) — so a decade of production servers ran with a backlog two orders of magnitude below the number in their source. On a LISTEN row ss repurposes the queue columns: Send-Q is the backlog you actually got, Recv-Q is how many connections are waiting for you right now.

quiz.prompt: Nothing is running on port 9000, but bind() fails with EADDRINUSE. What is holding the port, and why does that mechanism exist at all?

options.text: A closed connection in TIME_WAIT, held so late packets from the dead connection can't be delivered into a new one reusing the same numbers
options.why: The endpoint that closes first parks in TIME_WAIT for roughly twice the maximum segment lifetime. A connection is identified only by its four-tuple, so if you could immediately rebind and a delayed duplicate packet from the old connection arrived, it would be indistinguishable from data on the new one. TIME_WAIT is the interval that lets those strays die out first.

options.text: The kernel keeps the port reserved for a fixed cooldown after any process that bound it exits
options.why: There's no per-port cooldown tied to process exit. The lingering state belongs to individual connections that were closed, which is why the failure depends on whether a client ever connected and who closed first — not on how the process died.

options.text: The listening socket itself is still open, because killing a process doesn't close its sockets
options.why: Process death does close every fd it held, listening sockets included — and a server that only ever listened, with no connections through it, can be killed and restarted immediately with no error at all. It's a closed *connection* that lingers here, never the listener.

options.text: Another process on the machine grabbed the port in the moment between your two runs
options.why: Possible in principle, but it isn't what's happening in the reproducible case, and you can rule it out by looking: ss -tan (or /proc/net/tcp) will show the port in TIME_WAIT with no owning process rather than LISTEN under someone else's PID.

quiz.prompt: You hit EADDRINUSE, add SO_REUSEADDR, rebuild, and restart — and it fails again. The next restart works. What happened?

options.text: The rebuild reset the TIME_WAIT timer, so the second attempt simply waited it out
options.why: Compiling a binary can't touch kernel connection state, and TIME_WAIT runs for a minute or two — far longer than the gap between two restarts. If waiting it out were the explanation, the option would be irrelevant, and it isn't.

options.text: SO_REUSEADDR only applies to the second and later sockets a process creates, never the first
options.why: There's no such ordinal rule; the option is per-socket and applies to whichever socket you set it on, first or not. What matters is that the *other* socket in the conflict — the one in TIME_WAIT — also carries it.

options.text: Both the lingering TIME_WAIT socket and the new one need the flag, and the TIME_WAIT socket came from the previous run, which didn't set it
options.why: Accepted connections inherit their options from the listening socket that produced them, so the flag on the socket holding your port is whatever the *previous* binary set — not what you just compiled. The first restart after adding the option is therefore still refused; from the next run onward the lingering socket carries the flag too and it works forever after. This is a genuinely confusing hour if nobody warns you.

options.text: setsockopt() needs a moment to propagate, so the option isn't active on the very first bind after a rebuild
options.why: setsockopt() takes effect synchronously before it returns — there is no propagation delay anywhere in this path. The asymmetry comes from *which socket* carries the flag, not from timing.

quiz.prompt: SO_REUSEPORT is one letter different from SO_REUSEADDR and does something entirely different. What does it let you do that SO_REUSEADDR does not?

options.text: Let several separate processes bind the same port at once, with the kernel load-balancing incoming connections across them
options.why: Added in Linux 3.9 (2013), and it's how you scale accepting across cores without one thread doing all the accept()ing and handing work off: run N identical processes, each with its own listening socket on port 80, and the kernel distributes connections by hashing the four-tuple. It also gives you zero-downtime restarts, since the new process can bind before the old one exits. NGINX, HAProxy and Envoy all expose a flag for it.

options.text: Bind one socket to several ports at once, so a server can listen on 80 and 443 with a single fd
options.why: A socket has exactly one local endpoint; nothing in the API binds one fd to multiple ports. Serving both 80 and 443 means two listening sockets, and then multiplexing between them with poll/epoll.

options.text: Bind to the same port on several different network interfaces at once
options.why: You already get that from INADDR_ANY, with no special option at all — one socket bound to the wildcard address receives on every interface. REUSEPORT is about multiple *sockets* sharing one port, not one socket spanning interfaces.

options.text: Reuse a port still held in TIME_WAIT, without waiting the timer out
options.why: That's SO_REUSEADDR's job — the option you're already using. The names being one letter apart is exactly why these get confused, but they solve unrelated problems.

days.title: accept()
days.teaser: Two fds, one connection. The single most-missed fact in hand-rolled socket code.
days.teachBack: Explain why accept() returns a new fd instead of reusing the listening one. What is the listening socket doing while you're talking to a client, and what breaks if you close the wrong one?
days.theoryMarkdown:
### Two file descriptors, one connection

```cpp
sockaddr_in peer{};
socklen_t len = sizeof(peer);
int conn = accept(listen_fd, reinterpret_cast<sockaddr *>(&peer), &len);
```

`accept()` hands back a **new** fd. Your listening fd is untouched and still in `LISTEN`,
still collecting handshakes the kernel completes for you. The new one represents exactly
one conversation with exactly one client.

This is the single most-missed fact in hand-rolled socket code, and every bug that comes
from missing it looks baffling: servers that serve one client and then hang forever,
servers that die when a client disconnects, servers that accept a second connection onto
the first client's socket. All of them are the same mistake — treating the two fds as
interchangeable.

If you only remember one sentence from this milestone, make it this one: **the listening
socket is a factory, the accepted socket is a product.** You close products when you're
done with them. You do not close the factory.

### Why a new fd is the only design that works

The deeper answer is about how TCP identifies a connection at all. A connection is not
named by a port. It's named by a **four-tuple**: local IP, local port, remote IP, remote
port. All four together.

So when three clients connect to your server, you get three connected sockets that all
share the *same* local port 9000, and differ only in the remote half:

```
127.0.0.1:9000  <->  127.0.0.1:51234
127.0.0.1:9000  <->  127.0.0.1:51235
127.0.0.1:9000  <->  127.0.0.1:51236
```

Port 9000 is not "used up" by the first client, and it never gets divided between them.
That's also why a busy web server can hold sixty thousand simultaneous connections on
port 443 without running out of anything port-shaped. Each of those needs its own kernel
socket object — its own buffers, its own sequence numbers, its own state machine — and
therefore its own fd. There is nowhere else for them to live.

### The kernel fills in the address for you

The second and third arguments are how you find out who connected. You pass a buffer and
*a pointer to* its size; the kernel writes the peer's address into the buffer and writes
the number of bytes it actually used back through the pointer.

That in-and-out parameter is called a **value-result** argument, and it's all over this
API for one reason: C can't return two things. You must initialise `len` to the size of
your buffer before the call — passing an uninitialised `socklen_t` is a real and
irritating bug, because it often "works" by accident when the stack garbage happens to
be large enough.

If you don't care who connected, both arguments can be `nullptr`.

To print the address, use `inet_ntop()` and not `inet_ntoa()` — Day 2 covered why the
older one hands you a pointer into a static buffer that the next call overwrites.

### accept4(), and Day 1's race again

Linux has `accept4()`, which takes the same arguments plus a flags word:

```cpp
int conn = accept4(listen_fd, nullptr, nullptr, SOCK_CLOEXEC);
```

This is exactly the `SOCK_CLOEXEC` problem from Day 1, one level up. Close-on-exec is
*not* inherited from the listening socket, so every connection you accept starts life
inheritable by any program you `exec()`. Setting it afterwards with `fcntl()` reopens the
same nanosecond race Day 1 described. `accept4()` closes it by doing both in one syscall.

`SOCK_NONBLOCK` is the other flag it takes, and that one becomes interesting the moment
you have an event loop — milestone 02's problem rather than today's.

### What blocking actually means here

Your `accept()` will block. The process stops, the kernel deschedules it, and it consumes
no CPU at all while waiting — this is a sleep, not a spin. When a connection lands in the
accept queue, the kernel wakes you and `accept()` returns.

That's fine for one client at a time and completely useless for many, which is the
motivation for most of the rest of this curriculum. It's also the origin of a classic
piece of systems folklore: if several processes are blocked in `accept()` on the *same*
listening socket and one connection arrives, older kernels woke all of them, and all but
one immediately went back to sleep having found nothing. That's the **thundering herd**;
modern Linux wakes only one, but the phrase outlived the bug and now gets used for any
stampede-on-a-single-event problem.

### Go and look at both sockets

With a client connected, your process holds two sockets on port 9000 in different
states. They show up separately:

```console
$ ss -tan | grep 9000
LISTEN  0  4096   0.0.0.0:9000    0.0.0.0:*
ESTAB   0  0    127.0.0.1:9000  127.0.0.1:51234
```

One row is the factory, still listening. The other is the product — same local port,
different remote address, which is the four-tuple made visible. `/proc/<pid>/fd` from
Day 1 shows them as two separate `socket:[...]` entries with different inode numbers.

quiz.prompt: accept() returns a new fd rather than reusing the listening one. What is the listening socket doing while you're talking to a client, and what breaks if you close the wrong one?

options.text: It stays in LISTEN collecting new handshakes; close it and the server can never accept again, though the current client keeps working
options.why: The listening socket is a factory and the accepted socket is a product. The kernel keeps completing handshakes into the accept queue the whole time you're busy with a client. Closing the listener leaves the current conversation perfectly healthy — which is exactly what makes the bug confusing, because it looks fine until the *second* client never connects.

options.text: It's idle and does nothing until you call accept() again, so closing it early is harmless
options.why: The kernel is answering SYNs and completing three-way handshakes on that socket continuously, with no involvement from your code — that's what Day 3's accept queue is filling up with. It is never idle while it's in LISTEN.

options.text: It holds the shared receive buffer that every client's data arrives in, so closing it loses in-flight data
options.why: Buffers are per-connection, living on the accepted socket, not pooled on the listener. A listening socket never carries application data at all — it only ever produces new connections.

options.text: It becomes the connection once accept() returns, so the returned fd is really just a duplicate of it
options.why: They're two distinct kernel objects with different states and different buffers — /proc/<pid>/fd shows different inode numbers, and ss shows one row in LISTEN and another in ESTAB. Treating them as duplicates is precisely the mistake this day exists to prevent.

quiz.prompt: Three clients are connected to your server on port 9000 at the same time. What distinguishes their three connections from each other, given they share a local port?

options.text: The four-tuple — local IP, local port, remote IP, remote port. Only the remote half differs, and that's enough
options.why: A connection is identified by all four values together, never by a port alone. That's why port 9000 isn't consumed by the first client and never gets divided up, and why a busy server can hold tens of thousands of simultaneous connections on a single port without running out of anything port-shaped.

options.text: Nothing distinguishes them at the TCP layer; the application has to tag each message to tell clients apart
options.why: Backwards — the demultiplexing is precisely what TCP does for you. The kernel routes each arriving segment to the right socket by matching the four-tuple, which is why recv() on one client's fd never returns another client's bytes.

options.text: The fd number is what identifies the connection to the kernel
options.why: The fd is your process's private handle, meaningful only inside your fd table — another process can hold fd 5 for something entirely unrelated. TCP identifies the connection on the wire by the four-tuple; the fd never leaves your machine.

options.text: The kernel assigns each accepted connection a different local port behind the scenes
options.why: The server's local port stays 9000 on every accepted connection — you can see it directly in ss, where several ESTAB rows share the same local address and port. It's the *client* that uses a fresh ephemeral port per connection.

quiz.prompt: The socklen_t argument to accept() is passed by pointer rather than by value. Why — and what goes wrong if you forget to initialise it?

options.text: So accept() can resize your buffer with realloc() if the peer address doesn't fit
options.why: The kernel never allocates or reallocates memory in your process — it only writes into the buffer you supplied, and truncates if it's too small. Nothing in this API takes ownership of your storage.

options.text: It's a value-result argument: you pass in your buffer's size, the kernel writes back the size it used. Uninitialised, the kernel sees stack garbage as your buffer size
options.why: C can't return two things, so the API borrows the caller's variable to carry a value in each direction — a pattern that recurs all over these calls. Leaving it uninitialised is nasty precisely because it often appears to work: whenever the garbage happens to be large enough, the kernel fills the address normally, so the bug hides until the day the stack contains something small.

options.text: Because socklen_t is too large to pass in a register on most architectures
options.why: socklen_t is a 32-bit integer; passing it by value would be trivial. The pointer exists for the return direction, not for the argument direction.

options.text: It's a legacy quirk with no effect — passing nullptr for the length works identically
options.why: Passing nullptr for *both* the address and the length is legal and means "I don't care who connected". Passing a real address buffer with a null or uninitialised length is not the same thing, and is a genuine bug.

quiz.prompt: What does accept4(fd, ..., SOCK_CLOEXEC) give you that accept() followed by fcntl(F_SETFD, FD_CLOEXEC) does not?

options.text: It sets close-on-exec on the listening socket too, covering both fds at once
options.why: accept4()'s flags apply to the newly created connection only. The listening socket's flags are whatever you set when you created it, and are unaffected.

options.text: It makes the connection non-blocking as well, which FD_CLOEXEC does not
options.why: That's a different flag — SOCK_NONBLOCK, which accept4() also accepts. SOCK_CLOEXEC controls only what survives an exec(); it has no effect on whether reads and writes block.

options.text: Atomicity — between accept() returning and fcntl() running, another thread can fork+exec and leak the connection to the child
options.why: Exactly the race from Day 1, one level up. Close-on-exec is not inherited from the listening socket, so every accepted connection starts life inheritable, and the two-call fix has a window measured in instructions. On a server accepting thousands of connections a second while also spawning helpers, that window gets hit. accept4() collapses both into one syscall.

options.text: Nothing functionally — accept4() is just a convenience that saves you typing a second call
options.why: The convenience is real but incidental; the reason the flag was added to the creating call was the race, not ergonomics. That's the same motivation behind pipe2(), dup3() and open()'s O_CLOEXEC.

quiz.prompt: Your process is blocked in accept() with no clients connecting. What is it costing the machine while it waits?

options.text: A full CPU core, since accept() polls the accept queue in a tight loop
options.why: Nothing in the blocking path spins. You can watch this directly: a server parked in accept() sits at 0% CPU in top no matter how long it waits.

options.text: Essentially nothing — the kernel deschedules the process, so it burns no CPU until a connection arrives
options.why: Blocking here is a sleep, not a spin: the process leaves the run queue entirely and the scheduler wakes it when the accept queue gets an entry. What it does cost is the thread and its stack — which is fine for one client and hopeless for ten thousand, and is the whole reason readiness notification (select, poll, epoll) and this curriculum's later milestones exist.

options.text: One kernel thread per waiting socket, scheduled alongside your process
options.why: The kernel doesn't spawn a thread to babysit a waiting socket; your own process's thread is simply parked on a wait queue attached to the socket, and the arriving connection wakes it.

options.text: Nothing at all — a blocked process is completely free, which is why one-thread-per-connection scales fine
options.why: The CPU cost is genuinely near zero, but "completely free" is the trap. Each blocked thread still holds its stack (commonly 8 MB of reserved address space) and adds scheduler bookkeeping — which is precisely why thread-per-connection collapses long before readiness-based designs do.

days.title: recv() and send(), once each
days.teaser: Read the same bytes twice without consuming them, and prove the kernel's buffer is not yours.
days.teachBack: What does the return value of recv() mean — all three cases. Then: your buffer is 1024 bytes and the client sent 4000. Walk through what actually happens, and where the other bytes are in the meantime.
days.theoryMarkdown:
### The return value is a count, not a message

```cpp
ssize_t n = recv(fd, buf, sizeof(buf), 0);
```

`recv()` returns the number of bytes it put in your buffer. Not "a message", not "the
thing the client sent" — a count of bytes, and it can be smaller than what you asked for
and smaller than what the client sent in one go.

Three outcomes, and all three must be handled:

- **`n > 0`** — that many bytes are in your buffer. Nothing more is promised. In
  particular there is no null terminator, so treating `buf` as a C string without
  writing one yourself reads whatever was in memory after the data.
- **`n == 0`** — **orderly shutdown**. The peer sent a FIN: they have closed their
  sending side and no more data will ever arrive on this connection. This is not an
  error, and it is not "nothing arrived yet" — a blocking `recv()` never returns 0 for
  "wait a moment". Zero means end of stream, permanently.
- **`n < 0`** — error, with the reason in `errno`. `ECONNRESET` means the peer's end
  died rudely (an RST rather than a FIN). `EINTR` means a signal interrupted the call
  before any data arrived, and you should simply call it again.

The 0-versus-negative distinction is the one that matters most, because they demand
opposite reactions: `0` is a normal end-of-conversation you should close cleanly on,
`-1` is a failure you should report. Code that lumps them together as "the loop is over"
silently swallows real errors.

`send()` mirrors it, and has the same trap in the other direction: **its return value is
how many bytes it actually accepted**, which can be fewer than you asked it to send.
That's Day 6's problem, but the return value is the same kind of promise — a count, not
an acknowledgement.

Neither call tells you anything about whether the data reached the other machine.
`send()` returning 512 means 512 bytes are now in the kernel's send buffer and are the
kernel's problem. It does not mean they arrived, and there is no socket API call that
tells you they did.

### The kernel's buffer is not your buffer

Every socket has receive and send buffers in kernel memory (Day 1's list). Bytes arrive
from the network into the receive buffer whether or not your process ever calls
`recv()`, and `recv()` copies from that buffer into yours and *removes* what it copied.

You can prove this in two lines with a flag most people never learn, `MSG_PEEK`, which
copies without consuming:

```cpp
recv(fd, buf, sizeof(buf), MSG_PEEK);   // look
recv(fd, buf, sizeof(buf), MSG_PEEK);   // look again — identical bytes
recv(fd, buf, sizeof(buf), 0);          // now actually take them
recv(fd, buf, sizeof(buf), MSG_DONTWAIT); // -1, EAGAIN — the buffer is empty
```

Run that and the first two calls return the same bytes and the same count. Nothing about
the connection changed between them; the data was sitting in kernel memory the whole
time, and "reading" is a copy-and-remove operation, not an event.

`MSG_PEEK` is genuinely useful beyond the demo: protocol dispatchers use it to look at
the first few bytes and decide which handler should own the connection before any of the
data has been consumed. It's also a good way to lose an afternoon, because peeking in a
loop while waiting for more data is a busy-wait that will happily spin a core.

Two other flags worth knowing exist:

- **`MSG_WAITALL`** — don't return until the full requested count has arrived (or the
  connection ends). It turns the short-read problem off for a fixed-size read, and it's
  the right tool when you genuinely know the length in advance.
- **`MSG_DONTWAIT`** — make just this one call non-blocking, returning `EAGAIN` rather
  than sleeping. Per-call, so you don't have to change the socket's mode.

### Why a short read is normal, not an error

You ask for 1024 bytes; the client sent 4000. `recv()` gives you, say, 1448 — or 512, or
73. It returns what's in the receive buffer *now* rather than waiting for more, because
TCP is a stream and there is no "rest of the message" for it to wait for: it has no idea
where your message ends. Bytes arrive in whatever chunks the network and the sender's
kernel produced, and those chunks have nothing to do with the sizes the sender passed to
`send()`.

Today you call `recv()` exactly once and see this happen. Tomorrow you loop, which is
where it stops being a curiosity and starts being a bug you have to design against.

quiz.prompt: What does recv() returning 0 mean, and why is it a different situation from returning -1?

options.text: 0 means your buffer size was 0; with a non-empty buffer recv() only ever returns positive or -1
options.why: A zero-length buffer is a degenerate case, but a normal recv() on a normal buffer genuinely does return 0 the moment the peer closes its sending side — it's the standard, expected way you learn a client hung up.

options.text: 0 is an orderly shutdown — the peer sent FIN and no more data will ever arrive. -1 is an error with the reason in errno
options.why: They demand opposite reactions: 0 is a normal end of conversation you close cleanly on, -1 is a failure you report. A blocking recv() never returns 0 to mean "nothing yet" — zero is permanent end of stream. Code that collapses both into "the loop is over" silently swallows real errors like ECONNRESET.

options.text: 0 means no data was available yet, so you should call recv() again in a moment
options.why: That's what a blocking recv() will never do — it sleeps until something arrives rather than returning empty-handed. The "nothing yet" answer is -1 with EAGAIN, and only on a non-blocking socket or with MSG_DONTWAIT.

options.text: 0 means the connection failed, and -1 means it closed normally
options.why: Exactly inverted. It's worth fixing this one firmly, because getting it backwards produces a server that treats every clean disconnect as an error and every error as a clean disconnect.

quiz.prompt: You call recv(fd, buf, 1024, 0) and the client sent 4000 bytes. What can you say about the return value, and where are the remaining bytes?

options.text: It returns somewhere between 1 and 1024 — whatever is in the receive buffer now — and the rest stays in the kernel's buffer for later calls
options.why: recv() returns what's available rather than waiting for a total it has no way to know, because TCP is a stream with no message boundaries. It can hand back far less than either your buffer size or the sender's write size: the chunks you see come from the network and the sender's kernel, not from the sender's send() calls. This is the short read, and Day 6 is about designing for it.

options.text: It returns 4000, since the kernel reassembles the whole message before waking you
options.why: It can't return more than the buffer size you passed, and there is no "message" for the kernel to reassemble — it has no idea where the sender thought one ended. TCP guarantees order and delivery, never framing.

options.text: It returns exactly 1024, because recv() always fills the buffer it's given if enough data exists
options.why: Only MSG_WAITALL asks for that behaviour, and even it gives up early if the connection ends. A plain recv() is explicitly permitted to return less, and on a real network routinely does — often at odd sizes like 1448, the payload that fits one Ethernet frame.

options.text: It returns -1 with EMSGSIZE, since the incoming data doesn't fit the buffer
options.why: Oversized data isn't an error condition on a stream socket at all. The excess simply stays in the receive buffer and is delivered by subsequent calls; the data is only dropped if you close the connection without reading it.

quiz.prompt: send() returns 512 when you asked it to send 512 bytes. What has actually happened at that point, and what has not?

options.text: The bytes were written directly to the network card, bypassing kernel buffering for small writes
options.why: There's no such bypass in the ordinary path; everything goes through the socket send buffer, where TCP decides on segmentation and timing (Nagle, congestion window, and the rest). Kernel-bypass stacks exist but are a specialist tool, not what send() does.

options.text: The peer's kernel has acknowledged all 512 bytes, though the peer's application may not have read them
options.why: Closer to the truth than "the app read it", but still more than send() promises. send() can return long before any ACK comes back — it returns as soon as the data is copied into the send buffer.

options.text: 512 bytes are in the kernel's send buffer and are now its problem — it does not mean they reached the peer, and no socket call tells you that
options.why: send() is a handoff to the kernel, not a delivery receipt. The bytes may still be queued, in flight, or lost and awaiting retransmission. This is why application-level acknowledgements exist: if your protocol needs to know the other side actually got something, the other side has to say so.

options.text: The peer's application has received all 512 bytes
options.why: Two layers too optimistic. Even after the bytes genuinely arrive, they sit in the peer's receive buffer until its code calls recv() — which it may never do.

quiz.prompt: Two consecutive MSG_PEEK reads return the same bytes. What does that tell you about where the data lives and what a normal recv() does?

options.text: The peer sent the data twice, once for each peek
options.why: Nothing goes back to the peer when you call recv() — MSG_PEEK generates no network traffic whatsoever. The sender has no idea whether or how often you've read.

options.text: It means the socket is in a special peek mode until you clear it with a normal read
options.why: MSG_PEEK is a per-call flag with no lasting effect on the socket. You can freely interleave peeking and normal reads; nothing is latched.

options.text: The data sits in a kernel-side receive buffer, and a normal recv() is a copy-and-remove from it — peeking copies without removing
options.why: This is the whole mental model in one experiment. Bytes arrive into kernel memory whether or not you ever call recv(); reading is not an event you're notified of, it's you taking a copy and consuming it. Once you see the same bytes twice and then watch a plain recv() make them disappear, short reads and buffering stop being abstract.

options.text: MSG_PEEK caches the bytes in your process, so the second read comes from a userspace copy
options.why: There's no userspace cache in the C library here; each peek is a syscall that copies out of the same kernel buffer. That's why the data survives — it was never removed from the kernel's side.

quiz.prompt: Your code does buf[n] = '\0' after a successful recv() and prints buf as a string. What is the assumption there, and when does it bite?

options.text: That n < sizeof(buf) — if recv() filled the buffer completely, that write is one past the end
options.why: A classic off-by-one buffer overflow, and it hides for a long time because it only triggers when a read happens to fill the buffer exactly. Either pass sizeof(buf) - 1 as the length so the terminator always fits, or stop treating network bytes as a C string and print exactly n bytes — the data has no terminator of its own and may legitimately contain zero bytes anywhere.

options.text: That recv() null-terminates the data itself, making the assignment redundant
options.why: recv() never terminates anything — it delivers exactly the bytes that arrived. The assignment is necessary if you insist on C-string handling; it's the lack of a bounds check that's the bug, not the assignment.

options.text: Nothing is assumed — writing at index n is always safe because recv() returns at most sizeof(buf)
options.why: "At most sizeof(buf)" is exactly the problem: when n equals sizeof(buf), index n is the first byte past the end. The bound you need is one smaller than the bound recv() respects.

options.text: That the peer sent text rather than binary, which is only a display problem
options.why: Real, but not the dangerous part. Printing binary as text is ugly; writing past the end of the buffer is memory corruption, which is a different class of problem entirely.
